peabiru

Travel-time matrices, accessibility, isochrones and detailed itineraries by walking, cycling, driving and public transport, with fares, slope costs and scenarios, on networks built from an OpenStreetMap extract, GTFS public transport feeds and an optional elevation raster. It is a Rust port of Conveyal’s R5 routing engine. The routing engine is written in Rust and runs inside the R session: no Java is needed, and the network is built once, in memory, and reused by every call. The same engine is behind the Python and JavaScript packages and the command-line tool of the same name.

Authorship. peabiru is an independent project. Its routing model is that of Conveyal’s R5, and its fare calculator and parts of its trip planner are translated from r5r (Ipea); both are MIT-licensed, and their notices are kept in LICENSE-THIRD-PARTY. peabiru is not affiliated with or endorsed by Conveyal, Ipea or the r5r team. The port was written with the assistance of AI coding tools.

Website: https://strategicprojects.github.io/peabiru-routing/ (this package’s documentation is at https://strategicprojects.github.io/peabiru-routing/r/).

Function What it computes
build_network() a network from one .pbf, any number of GTFS feeds and an optional elevation raster (.tif)
travel_time_matrix() travel times by "WALK", "BICYCLE", "CAR" or public transport ("TRANSIT" or any of its modes, reached by walking, bicycle or car), with percentiles over a departure window
accessibility() opportunities reachable from each origin, with five decay functions
expanded_travel_time_matrix() the trip of every departure minute, with its breakdown
arrival_travel_time_matrix() the latest trip that arrives by a given time
isochrone() the areas or street segments reached within each cutoff
detailed_itineraries() the legs of each trip, with their lines (the fastest trip, or the alternatives)
setup_fare_structure(), read_fare_structure(), write_fare_structure() fare structures, which the routing functions take as fare_structure
pareto_frontier() the trade-off between travel time and fare
find_snap(), street_network_bbox(), street_network_to_sf(), transit_network_to_sf() where points snap, and the street and transit networks as sf
check_transit_availability(), get_gtfs_errors() the dates with service, and the errors in the GTFS feeds

The routing functions also take scenarios of car speeds (new_carspeeds, carspeed_scale) and of traffic stress for cyclists (new_lts). What peabiru does not support stops with an error that says so, for instance a fare structure that names a fare calculator (a type) instead of fare rules; nothing is silently ignored.

Installation

From GitHub, with Rust installed (cargo and rustc 1.81 or later):

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("StrategicProjects/peabiru-routing@r-package")

# or, with remotes
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("StrategicProjects/peabiru-routing@r-package")

The branch r-package holds the released package with the sources of the routing engine, so nothing else is downloaded while it compiles (about a minute). The development version is in the directory r/ of the branch main: clone the repository and run R CMD INSTALL r.

Example 

library(peabiru)

data_path <- system.file("extdata/spo", package = "peabiru")
network <- build_network(data_path)
points <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "spo_points.csv"))

ttm <- travel_time_matrix(
  network, points, points,
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo"),
  percentiles = c(25, 50, 75),
  seed = 42
)

Class of the results

The functions return tibbles by default (sf tibbles for the results with a geometry). options(peabiru.output = "data.frame") gives base data frames and options(peabiru.output = "data.table") data.tables; the rows, columns and values are the same whatever the class. There is also a comparison with r5r.

Documentation

The package website is built from this directory with pkgdown, together with the rest of the project’s documentation: run site/build.sh at the root of the repository and open _site/r/index.html. It has a getting-started vignette and articles on travel-time matrices, accessibility, expanded and arrival matrices, detailed itineraries, fares, elevation, scenarios, inspecting a network, how the engine works, and benchmarks. To go from points to maps with sf, dplyr and ggplot2, start with “peabiru with sf and the tidyverse”: an sf grid in any coordinate reference system, the routing functions with the native pipe, dplyr on the tibbles they return, joins back to the geometry and geom_sf() maps.

Licence and credits

MIT. The routing model follows Conveyal’s R5 (MIT), from which the routing logic is ported. The functions are modelled on those of r5r (MIT, Ipea): the fare calculator and parts of the trip planner are translated from its Java code, many functions share their names, arguments and result layouts with r5r’s, and the sample network is cut from the São Paulo sample data of the r5r project.

The notices of the works peabiru derives from are in inst/LICENSE-THIRD-PARTY. The package’s compiled code also contains Rust crates by other authors (extendr, miniz_oxide and others): they are listed in inst/AUTHORS, with their licence texts in inst/LICENSE-RUST-CRATES.
